::: {.callout-note}
## About this page
This is what a lesson looks like to a learner. Its source is
[`vignettes/example-lesson.qmd`](https://github.com/ryjohnson09/quarto-simulator/blob/main/vignettes/example-lesson.qmd).
The other vignettes explain how each part is written.
:::

A Quarto document is plain text with three parts: a **YAML header** that sets
document options, **markdown** prose, and **code cells** that run when the
document renders.

Each playground below has an editor on the left and the rendered document on
the right. The preview is a simulation of Quarto that runs in your browser,
made for practising the basics. Edit the text, then press **▶ Render** (or <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>/<kbd>Cmd</kbd>
\+ <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>K</kbd>, the same shortcut RStudio uses) to see the result.
Everything runs in your browser.

## Explore

Try changing the title, adding `toc: true` to the YAML header, or changing
`cars` to `pressure` in the code cell.

````{quarto-simulator}
---
title: "Stopping distances"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
---

## Introduction

The `cars` dataset records the speed of cars and the distances taken to stop.
It has `{r} nrow(cars)` rows.

::: {.callout-note}
These data were recorded in the 1920s.
:::

## Analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-cars
#| fig-cap: "Stopping distance increases with speed."
plot(cars, xlab = "Speed (mph)", ylab = "Stopping distance (ft)")
abline(lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars), col = "steelblue")
```

As @fig-cars shows, faster cars take longer to stop.
````

## Exercise 1: Document options and callouts

The YAML header controls how the whole document renders. Update this document so that:

1. It has a **table of contents**.
2. The sentence about practice is inside a **tip callout**.

````{quarto-simulator}
#| exercise: ex-toc
---
title: "Learning Quarto"
---

## Why Quarto?

Quarto weaves together prose and code.

## Getting started

Practice makes perfect: render early and often.

## Next steps

Try a callout of your own.
````

::: {.hint exercise="ex-toc"}
A table of contents is a document option, so it goes in the YAML header between the `---` lines.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex-toc"}
A callout is a fenced div with a class: start it with `::: {.callout-tip}` and end it with `:::`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-toc"}
```markdown
---
title: "Learning Quarto"
toc: true
---

## Why Quarto?

Quarto weaves together prose and code.

## Getting started

::: {.callout-tip}
Practice makes perfect: render early and often.
:::

## Next steps

Try a callout of your own.
```
:::

```{quarto-simulator-check}
#| exercise: ex-toc
if (result.yaml.toc !== true) {
  return fail("The document doesn't have a table of contents yet. Which YAML option turns one on?")
}
const tip = result.html.querySelector(".callout-tip")
if (!tip) {
  return fail("There's no tip callout yet. Wrap the practice sentence in `::: {.callout-tip}` … `:::`.")
}
if (!tip.textContent.includes("Practice makes perfect")) {
  return fail("You have a tip callout, but it doesn't contain the sentence about practice.")
}
return pass("Your document has a table of contents and a tip callout.")
```

## Exercise 2: Code cell options

Cell options start with `#|` and go at the top of a code cell. Change the cell so that:

1. The **code is hidden** and only the plot shows.
2. The plot is a **cross-referenceable figure**: give it a label starting with `fig-` and a caption.
3. The sentence below the cell **refers to the figure** with `@`.

````{quarto-simulator}
#| exercise: ex-cells
---
title: "Air pressure"
---

```{r}
plot(pressure, type = "b")
```

The plot above shows that vapor pressure rises steeply with temperature.
````

::: {.hint exercise="ex-cells"}
`#| echo: false` hides a cell's code. Figures need both `#| label: fig-something` and `#| fig-cap: "..."`.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex-cells"}
Refer to a figure by its label, for example `@fig-pressure`. Quarto replaces it with "Figure 1".
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-cells"}
````markdown
---
title: "Air pressure"
---

```{r}
#| label: fig-pressure
#| fig-cap: "Vapor pressure of mercury by temperature."
#| echo: false
plot(pressure, type = "b")
```

@fig-pressure shows that vapor pressure rises steeply with temperature.
````
:::

```{quarto-simulator-check}
#| exercise: ex-cells
const cell = result.cells.find(c => c.lang === "r")
if (!cell) return fail("The R code cell is missing. Did it get deleted?")
if (cell.options.echo !== false) return fail("The code is still showing. Which cell option hides it?")
const figure = result.html.querySelector('[id^="fig-"]')
if (!figure) return fail("The plot isn't a cross-referenceable figure yet. Give the cell a `label` that starts with `fig-`.")
if (!cell.options["fig-cap"]) return fail("Add a `fig-cap` so the figure has a caption.")
if (!result.html.querySelector("a.quarto-xref")) {
  return fail("The text doesn't refer to the figure yet. Use `@` followed by the figure's label.")
}
return pass("The code is hidden, and the text refers to the figure by number.")
```

## Exercise 3: Fix the YAML

YAML is strict about indentation and punctuation. This document won't render.
Press **▶ Render**, read the error message, and fix the header.

````{quarto-simulator}
#| exercise: ex-yaml
---
title: "Quarterly report
author: Jordan
format:
  html:
  toc: true
---

## Summary

Sales were up this quarter.
````

::: {.hint exercise="ex-yaml"}
There are two problems. Check that every quote you open is closed. Options under `html:` need to be indented further than `html:` itself.
:::

```{quarto-simulator-check}
#| exercise: ex-yaml
if (result.yaml.title !== "Quarterly report") return fail("Check the title: it should read `Quarterly report`.")
if (result.yaml.format?.html?.toc !== true) {
  return fail("It renders now, but `toc: true` isn't an option of `html:` yet. Indent it under `html:`.")
}
if (!result.html.querySelector("nav#TOC")) return fail("The table of contents isn't showing yet.")
return pass("The YAML is valid, and the table of contents appears.")
```

## Exercise 4: Python cells

Python cells work too. Quarto runs them with Jupyter; here they run with
Python in your browser. Change the document so that:

1. The table is a **cross-referenceable table**: give the cell a label starting with `tbl-` and a `tbl-cap`.
2. The `???` is replaced by **inline Python code** that computes the average score, rounded to one decimal place.

````{quarto-simulator}
#| exercise: ex-python
---
title: "Quiz results"
---

```{python}
import pandas as pd
scores = pd.DataFrame({"student": ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"], "score": [88, 92, 79]})
scores
```

The average score was ???.
````

::: {.hint exercise="ex-python"}
Table options look like figure options: `#| label: tbl-scores` and `#| tbl-cap: "..."`.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex-python"}
Inline code is written `` `{python} expression` ``. Try `round(scores["score"].mean(), 1)`.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex-python"}
pandas returns NumPy numbers, which display as `np.float64(86.3)`. Format the number as
text instead: `` `{python} f"{scores['score'].mean():.1f}"` ``.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-python"}
````markdown
---
title: "Quiz results"
---

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scores
#| tbl-cap: "Quiz scores."
import pandas as pd
scores = pd.DataFrame({"student": ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"], "score": [88, 92, 79]})
scores
```

The average score was `{python} f"{scores['score'].mean():.1f}"`.
````
:::

```{quarto-simulator-check}
#| exercise: ex-python
const cell = result.cells.find(c => c.lang === "python")
if (!cell) return fail("The Python code cell is missing. Did it get deleted?")
if (!String(cell.options.label ?? "").startsWith("tbl-")) {
  return fail("The table isn't cross-referenceable yet. Give the cell a `label` that starts with `tbl-`.")
}
if (!cell.options["tbl-cap"]) return fail("Add a `tbl-cap` so the table has a caption.")
if (result.body.includes("???")) return fail("Replace `???` with inline Python code.")
if (!/(^|[^`])`\{python\}\s/m.test(result.body)) return fail("Use inline Python code rather than typing the number. It starts with a backtick and `{python}`.")
if (result.text.includes("np.float64")) {
  return fail("Python's number shows as `np.float64(...)`. Format it as text, for example with an f-string.")
}
if (!result.text.includes("86.3")) return fail("The average shows up, but it isn't 86.3 yet. Did you round to one decimal place?")
return pass("The table has a number and a caption, and the average is computed by Python.")
```
